title: Irish Stew
subtitle: Lamb neck chops simmered with potato and onion
excerpt: The simplest lamb stew: neck chops, potato, onion, and stock simmered together until the potato has thickened the broth and the lamb is falling off the bone. No browning, no extra steps.
sourceNotes: Irish stew appears in cookbooks and travellers' accounts from the eighteenth century. The traditional version contains only lamb (or mutton), potato, and onion: carrots and other vegetables are a later addition disputed by purists. Florence Irwin, The Cookin' Woman: Irish Country Recipes (1949) and Theodora FitzGibbon, A Taste of Ireland (1968) both emphasise the three-ingredient simplicity.

recipe.freezeNotes: The potato breaks down if frozen and the stew becomes grainy on reheating. Best eaten fresh or within two days.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Can be made a day ahead. The flavour improves but the potato becomes very soft. Add more liquid when reheating.

content.text: Irish stew is one of the simplest meat dishes in the British and Irish repertoire: lamb neck, potato, and onion covered with stock and simmered until the potato dissolves into the broth and the meat falls from the bone. There is no browning, no roux, no wine. The potato thickens the stew naturally. What it asks for is time.

The traditional argument is that Irish stew should contain only lamb, potato, and onion. Carrot is sometimes added but is considered a compromise by purists. If you want the classic, keep it to three main ingredients.

items.prepNote: floury variety, peeled and cut into chunks

content.text: Season the {{lamb-neck}} of neck chops generously with salt and pepper.
Layer the lamb chops, {{onion}} of onion, and {{carrot}} of carrot in a large saucepan. Pour over {{stock-lamb}} of stock. Add the thyme sprigs and bring slowly to a simmer.
Skim off any grey foam that rises in the first 10 minutes. Partially cover the pan and cook at a gentle simmer for 1 hour.
Add {{potato}} of potato chunks. Cook uncovered for a further 30 to 40 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the potato is completely soft and some of it has broken down into the broth to thicken it.
Remove the thyme sprigs. Taste and season. Serve in deep bowls with chopped parsley scattered over and bread to mop the bowl.

rows.cause: Floury potatoes break down to thicken the broth; waxy potatoes do not
rows.fix: Use a floury variety such as King Edward or Maris Piper. If the broth is still thin after 30 minutes of uncovered cooking with the potato, crush a few potato pieces against the side of the pan.

rows.cause: Simmer too gentle or chops were very thick
rows.fix: Continue cooking covered for another 30 minutes. Add a splash more stock if needed to keep the chops submerged.

content.text: Irish stew is the national dish of Ireland in the same way that fish and chips is British: not because of any formal designation but because it is the dish most people associate with Irish home cooking. It was a peasant dish built on the ingredients available in rural Ireland: mutton or lamb, potatoes, and onions. The simplicity is the point. It has survived precisely because it needs no skill, no equipment, and no expensive ingredients.
